utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and to those listening and following our procedures. I see you on your feet, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, and everyone. I just have a brief announcement and that is that we have an English translation for P2587. It's uploaded and available in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Tolimir has some issues with the microphone and with the headphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: If the Court Usher could assist, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, good morning to you again. And is everything now working? The microphone is not working. The Court Usher should assist him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine. I'm not receiving any interpretation. I can't hear, so I don't understand what you said, I don't understand what Mr. Vanderpuye answered to what you said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The Court Usher will assist you again, otherwise we have to call a technician. I would -- I think, not to waste time, we should call in a technician. I would kindly ask the Court Usher -- no, he's busy with that. Mr. Tolimir, are you now receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I am receiving interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, another issue? Or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. I just needed to correct the record. I misspoke. The exhibit number is 2857.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Document P2857 will now be received into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: So we are just trying again to understand. Mr. Tolimir, are you now receiving interpretation in a proper way?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Now I am receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If that problem occurs again, please let me know immediately. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic. Welcome back to the courtroom. Let me remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir is continuing his examination-in-chief. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May God's peace reign in this house and may these -- may God's will be done in these proceedings and not necessarily mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Skrbic. I wish you a pleasant stay in our midst and I wish that God's will may be done in these proceedings. Now my question: Did you have an opportunity to learn about the breakthrough through the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade while studying various documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber has had an opportunity to hear that the units of the Zvornik Brigade set an ambush near Djafin Kamen in Snagovo and finally in Baljkovica. The units of the Zvornik Brigade set up the first ambush near Djafin Kamen. The eye-witnesses say that they took the column by surprise and that they opened fire at close range and that there were a lot of casualties. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I presented that in my expert report. The data was taken over from witness statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Likewise, the eye-witnesses say that at Snagovo, in the Snagovo sector, an ambush was set up and that fire was opened from tanks, artillery, and anti-tank weapons and that fire was opened on two different columns of the BiH army which were breaking through from Snagovo towards the territory under the control of the enemy. That fire by the artillery units of the Drina Corps stopped because people could no longer watch people falling down in such great numbers. Were you aware that that happened in the Snagovo sector? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have to add to that that we're talking about two different columns that were moving in parallel to each other, about 70 metres apart from each other. Artillery fire was opened and there was all other sorts of support, but it doesn't make any difference because the distance between the two columns was only 70 metres and that the VRS had weapons and so did the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Their range was decreased because none of the weapons had been repaired in the meantime. I didn't know that fire stopped because the shooters could not watch people falling down in such great numbers. In military terms or from the military point of view, a fire opened on units that are breaking through is legitimate and fire can be opened from any weapons that are at the disposal of the unit that opens that fire. That fire has to be opened in such a way that people setting up the ambush have to be safe. This means that the quantity of the use of artillery, i.e., the amount of fire, has to be in keeping with the requirements of the safety of own people, those people that are setting up the ambush.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The combat situation that we have just discussed, i.e., fire opened from all the artillery weapons that one brigade has at its disposal, and that fire being opened on two columns, could this have caused major casualties as the witnesses here claim?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course that fire could indeed cause major losses, because those units were breaking through and not all the soldiers in the column were armed. They were just moving. In that column, they did not have any security on the flanks or any other support that may have guaranteed their safety. One cannot hide from artillery fire. The only protection is to dig in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could they dig in? Could they seek shelter in the ground if they were moving and if they were leaving one place in order to get to another? Did they have the time to dig in, to make shelters, to make fox holes?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that would have been contrary to the principles of a breakthrough. A breakthrough is primarily an attack activity, an assault activity, which does not imply digging in and making fox holes for protection. You do that only in a defence situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there were also great losses suffered by those elements that had dug in?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this concrete case, I did not have such information. However, in principle, entrenched units suffer fewer losses and they find it easier to protect themselves from artillery fire or any other fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information about the losses suffered by the forces at the head of that column that was breaking through in the sector of Snagovo and Baljkovica?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Among the total losses, there is very imprecise information as to how many were killed in combat in Srebrenica and around Srebrenica and how many were executed, so it's very difficult to make a distinction between those who were killed and those who were executed. There were, however, losses among the defenders of Srebrenica, i.e., among the units of the 28th Division, but it's very difficult to say how many. Simply, such information does not exist, save for the information that can be found in the 28th Division's report about the number of casualties covering the entire period of war, from 1992 to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have information about the losses of the Army of Republika Srpska in the sector where they set up those ambushes? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that sector, according to the report of the 2nd Corps command, if I'm not mistaken, the units of the Republika Srpska army suffered great losses. There were about 40 dead. Some eight or so were captured, they called them Chetniks. They also suffered losses in materiel. A few pieces of weaponry and ammunition were lost. That operation, the breakthrough operation, represented a major security risk not only for the Zvornik Brigade but also Zvornik as a settled area.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. You mostly relied on the BiH army sources.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at D280, which has been marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In order to save time, let's just look at the segments covering the period from the 12:09 to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir repeat the time references slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, please repeat the exact time. The interpreters didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The first segment is from 12:09 to 12:30. Then from 17:00 hours to 17:57. Then segment from 18:41 to 19:57. And finally, 33.2 [as interpreted] to 33:48. Thank you. I just quoted this time for the benefit of the technical personnel, and I will repeat the times again.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "How many? "How many do you think were killed? "Around two thousand. "Around two or three thousand at least. "At least. "There is no way I can describe what we experienced while we were breaking through; it's horrible for one to see or anything of the kind."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, do you want to see the beginning again, if you didn't hear it correctly?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I heard this and I was following the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who this person speaking is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document I can only recognise Mr. Golic. As far as I can remember, he was one of the commanders in the units of the 28th Division. I think he was a battalion commander, if I remember this correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned Golic as someone who was killed. Are these ABiH soldiers or VRS soldiers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are ABiH soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear what they were saying, how many were killed in the breakthrough or after the breakthrough? because this video was made after the breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They say that 2- to 3.000 were killed, at least. If they say "at least," that means that perhaps more people were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the excerpt from 17:00 to 17:57.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "That he killed himself! But he also killed the man next to him, who wouldn't have killed himself, and he wounded two others ... this was the first night on Buljim ... "Go ahead! "When the Chetniks rushed into the space where we were all gathered, when we arrived there early then we started ... do not film now ... um, we got there at about 12.00 in the evening. We went around ... at dusk in the bunker, not in the bunker, that's our camp, and this is where most people got killed. This is where they threw us in disarray. "What are the estimates? How many of you got killed? "There are, perhaps, two thousand missing, two or three, even more perhaps. I don't know how many exactly."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 15:57. That's the second excerpt.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, did you hear this participant and the information he provided? What was his estimate of the number of people who were killed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard him clearly. And he said that 2.000 or perhaps even more were killed. He doesn't know exactly. In this case, it's a member of the 28th Division from the column that was breaking through who was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did he mention the figure of 3.000 as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that 2- to 3.000 are missing, 2- to 3.000 combatants. When he says "missing," that means that they were either killed or were wounded somewhere. There were such cases, too. They couldn't have been aware of those cases, but he categorically stated that 2- to 3.000 were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the second excerpt, do the two speakers, the two participants, have the same estimates on losses sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And those are losses. That's the right term. In military doctrine, these are the terms that are used.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Have you already had the opportunity of seeing these videos and of listening to eye-witnesses providing information about the losses sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is the first time I have seen these videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see the following excerpt, the third one, from 18:41 to 19:57. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "I only saw one of them ... non stop. "... did he get across too? "Yes, he did ... and when we were going over Buljim ... "The Serbs were fleeing, crying ... "They ambushed us down there below Medica; we had them totally scattered in 15 minutes; we got hold of those two columns of people they wanted to cut off ... there were Mujo and these Golic men, the mountain battalion ... there are no men. Golic deserves to be general ... but he got killed yesterday ... they carried four ammunition belts and each carried an 84 -- M-84 machine-gun. "Let's go guys, up there, whoever can; the truck is waiting ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We stopped at 19 minutes and 57 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, when listening to these men from the ABiH speaking, did you hear anyone saying that there was an ambush that had been laid at Snagovo?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard someone mention an ambush laid in Buljim, but later it was said that there was an ambush at Snagovo, because Major Golic died in that ambush that had been laid at Snagovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So are we dealing with two ambushes; first one was laid in Buljim and then a second one in Snagovo? Is that what they are talking about, these speakers?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at the last excerpt, 33:02 to 33:48. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We had stayed an hour longer, not a day, an hour longer, had we stayed in the breakthrough, we would have been left ... "This is worse than hell ... "In two days we would have killed each other ... "Five or six thousand people ... "Last night, he threw a hand-grenade on the meadow and killed himself and wounded several other people. "He wounded ten people. "One man killed himself with a pistol ... he killed himself ... "We cannot explain this ... "He threw three hand-grenades ... "And did you see that guy who said, 'Guys, we have to go, I'm hungry' and he took out a hand-grenade and pulled the pin out? "That's nothing. "This morning, as he was sitting there, there was this young man next to me. There was a burst of fire and the man next to me got hit, that Gale from Glogova ... "And Masic barely managed to calm down ... but he's fine now, he's calmed down. An hour ago Masic said, 'Where are they chasing us away now? Is this collective surrender?'"

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we stopped at 13 -- at 33:48. My question is now as follows: Did you analyse documents in which reference was made about ABiH members who were breaking through from Srebrenica to Nezuk and Tuzla killing each other? Did you hear about such cases, of ABiH members mentioning the fact that they were killing each other?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I didn't search for such documents in particular, because these documents that speak about such members killing each other in the course of the Srebrenica battle and the breakthrough, well, such documents -- or so many documents don't really exist. But when I was looking at documents on the fighting of the 28th Division, I came across such information in other documents, information according to which they were killing each other. In the debriefing, for example, it says that in the course of the battle for Srebrenica they killed each other, they opened fire on a column that set off from Srebrenica to Potocari one day earlier than they should have, in my estimate, because they should have left on the 10th. And then here we saw that they were killing each other in the course of the breakthrough as well. There are a lot of reasons for which they did this, but there's no precise information as to the losses sustained by members of the 28th Division as a result of such internal conflicts. If I were to use the vocabulary that the Prosecutor uses, and his military expert Mr. Butler, for example, if I were to refer to several hundred, a thousand, more than a thousand, less than a thousand, and so on and so forth, well, if I were to express myself in such a manner, then I could say that in these internal conflicts several hundred, or perhaps over a thousand, or perhaps a thousand of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. You've heard all the information in these videos, so my question is as follows: Given the information you had obtained from the documents you saw, would you say that what these participants in the video said with regard to losses is accurate, since they provided very precise figures? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information provided by members of the 28th Division in these video extracts that we have just had a look at do no more than support the information that we referred to over the last few days. Information from the Secretary-General, for example, information from document P588, and this just confirms that there were about 3.000 or 3.000 [as interpreted] who were killed in the course of the breakthrough that the 28th Division of the ABiH attempted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness Skrbic. In the transcript, at page 13, line 3, you say the following. You spoke about the information provided by the members of the 28th Division in this video, but at the same time, a few minutes ago, if I'm not mistaken, you said that you had never seen this video before. Can you confirm that you have never seen this video before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So how is it that you know that these people who are speaking in the video are, in fact, members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you can see them. You can see in the video, in fact, that they are members of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it couldn't be anyone else. No one else attempted a breakthrough apart from the 28th Division, and here they are obviously speaking about the breakthrough from Srebrenica to Tuzla; therefore, they can't be members of some other unit, some other formation. They can only be members of the 28th Division that was making this breakthrough, regardless of whether they were wearing uniforms or whether they had arms or whether they were wearing civilian clothes. All those who took the decision to make that breakthrough took that decision together with their command, and they consciously decided to take the risk of breaking through. And as you heard yesterday, in item 4.1 in the document on the main ideas from the Supreme Command Staff, as you could see in that document, six or seven months prior to that event they were told that there might be a breakthrough and that a breakthrough is an extremely difficult and complex military operation. It's one of the most difficult and complex military operations. And it would be even more complex for them because they would have the people burdening them. They would be losing liberated territory and that wasn't mentioned for no reason, because if you lose liberated territory that means that you lose a source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You mentioned weapons, uniforms. I saw women in the video in civilian clothes. What would you say about these women in civilian clothes? Were they members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All I can say here is what my impression is when I look at these videos. My assumption is that the woman who appears in the video isn't a member of the 28th Division. I would say that she came from the team that welcomed the -- or waited for the members of the 28th Division. She was a part of the team supposed to assist them, so that's what my opinion of this woman who appears in the video is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, with regard to the losses referred to by the speakers in the video, and the figure of 3.000 is even mentioned, are those figures realistic ones for an operation that is called a breakthrough that was carried out 80 kilometres from the territory from which they departed when attempting this breakthrough?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are realistic figures. Under normal military circumstances, when you have a situation of an armed conflict, when a breakthrough is being attempted, then it would be quite realistic to expect to sustain even more significant losses. If you bear in mind the fact that of the 10- to 15.000 men fit for military service who set off with the 28th Division to carry out this breakthrough, only one-third of those men were armed, so the unarmed soldiers did not have adequate means for mounting a resistance or for carrying out the breakthrough; thus it was more realistic to expect them to sustain more significant losses than they actually did sustain. The fact that they only sustained the losses that they did sustain is due to the fact that the VRS didn't have sufficient forces to obstruct the axis of the breakthrough and to capture members of the 28th Division in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. In the documents that you had a look at, were you able to see any other references to the number mentioned by the men who appeared in the film?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have never seen in any of the other videos mention made of such significant losses. I only saw such references in the documents that I have already mentioned, and I won't repeat myself now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And in those other documents from other sources, written documents or documents of another kind, did those documents refer to any numbers? And if so, what figures were provided for the losses sustained?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I saw and examined such documents that I have already mentioned, and I said that the figure relating to the losses sustained in the course of the breakthrough was 3.000, about 3.000.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see D280 -- or, rather, could D280 be admitted into evidence. I apologise for tendering these documents, because this was the result of a situation that developed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you for a clarification. D280, you said this is marked for identification. What was the reason for that? This is number one. And the second question is: D280, is that the transcript of the text you can hear in the video or is it the video itself? Mr. Gajic, can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. D280 also has a supplementary sheet as well as a transcript. And it's under one number. It was marked for identification because when we were presenting this evidence through another witness, at the time we didn't have a complete transcript, and there were perhaps other reasons as well. But I hope that there is now a sufficient basis for this video and the transcript that pertains to the video now be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, I was told that the problem we have had recently was that no CD was provided to the Chamber and to the Prosecution of these parts you wanted to have into evidence. This is one part. The other is, Does the document that you are tendering only contain these parts we have seen on the screen today, these parts of the whole video, or does it contain more? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all let me say that this video contains more information. Of course, we didn't want to play the whole video in the courtroom because it lasts over an hour. We received this video from the Prosecution. There is no conversation taking place in the remaining part of the film that could have been transferred to a transcript. Now, looking at the images, I think that we all know very well what the situation was at the time in that area; therefore, we decided not to show it. Second question, with regard to the CD. The CD have been made, and during this session we are going to provide copies for the Prosecution and the Chamber because we have a sufficient number of them. In any case, we would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to admit the whole video-clip because this will set a context for the conversations that we saw in the excerpts that were played here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, we are only discussing a technical problem at the moment and this the CD. I was told by the Court Officer that the process of marking for identification was done only because the lack of a CD. Wait a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to correct myself: the only remaining condition. And after having received the CD you have just promised to provide us with, we will decide then. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Gajic. Can we now have D1119 [as interpreted] in e-court. And, Mr. President, if this document can be added to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you briefly explain what kind of document this is. Just mention the title, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is a bulletin, published by the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, its administration and military security service. And from this bulletin we are going to show only some pieces of information that this witness made reference to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it that the number in the transcript is not correct. It should be 1D1119. Mr. Vanderpuye, any objection to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add it to the list, Mr. Tolimir. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we please have first page in e-court, paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the document now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to speak into the microphone. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote, paragraph 1: "On the 16th of July, 1995, in the early evening hours, during the breakthrough of the main bulk of the forces of the 28th Division, around 10.000 members of the division arrived at a free territory. This breakthrough was assisted by units of the 24th Division that were carrying out a powerful counterattack on the Chetnik lines in the Baljkovica sector (the general area of Memici and Nezuk) at around 1700 hours, and linked up with the units of the 28th Division." Mr. Skrbic, yesterday when we were looking at the diagram that you showed us about the exit of the civilian population and members of the army from Srebrenica, you said that above this arrow you put the figure of 10.000 and that you yourself computed that number. Can you tell us whether the same number was precisely registered by the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina after the breakthrough operation of its forces from Srebrenica across the territory of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I am glad that you have showed me this document, because I didn't have access to it during my research. It supports the claim contained in my document, which is 10.632, above the arrow pointing from Kladanj to Tuzla. This figure, 10.632, are the civilians who joined the column of 25.000 men that was evacuated from Potocari to Tuzla. Now, from this paragraph one cannot say exactly that this figure coincides with the figure that I provided of 10.632, because there were not 10.000 members of the division, there were fewer of them. And now I am happy to say that this confirms that my calculation was correct, because even after the 16th of July members kept coming through whether they were armed or not. Now, thank you again for showing me this, because this corroborates my methodology of research, and I'm now convinced that it was completely proper. It was not difficult to reach the figure of 10.632 because if 25.000 people were evacuated from Potocari and the total of 35.632 of Muslims from Srebrenica were registered in Tuzla on the 4th of August, 1995, the registration accounting was done by the government from Sarajevo with the assistance of the WHO, then it is completely clear that this group of 25.000 must have been joined by some 10.632 people to make a total of 35.632 people. And they belonged, obviously, to the group that was carrying out the breakthrough. And thank you, once again, for giving me an opportunity to confirm my methodology.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Skrbic, you are talking very fast and you - again - you are overlapping. It's very difficult for the interpreters. Please pause between question and answer and the next question. And now continue, please, Mr. Tolimir. You started with a question. This is not recorded yet. Once again, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: On the front page of this bulletin, have you noticed that it was produced on the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can we please have the front page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll take a look at it now. Yes. At the bottom of this page it says that this document was made on the 17th of July, 1995, which is one day before the events represented in the document. I apologise, one day later after the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 2 of this bulletin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you spoke here about the civilians when you answered my question. Can you please look at line two.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have page 1. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Look at line two and -- or I'll read it again. [As read] "On the 16th of July, 1995, in the early evening hours, during the breakthrough of the main bulk of the 28th Division forces to the free territory, around 10.000 members of this division arrived there." Is the army treating them as civilians or as members of the military?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the BH army is treating them as being members of the division. There is no doubt about it. I would just like to add that one of the Muslim witnesses said that between 10.000 and 15.000 set off to carry out the breakthrough and that about 14.000 of those able-bodied men were members of the 28th Division. I can give you the name of this person, of this witness, but since I am not very skillful in deciding which witnesses are protected and which witnesses are not, I am not going to name any names to avoid disclosing any details about a potentially protected witness, although I have to admit that in my view every witness that testified with protective measures had a pseudonym and those who testify under their full names and with their full personal details are actually not protected witnesses and that what they testified about can be disclosed in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can this document D1119 be admitted into evidence, pending translation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, how many pages does this document contain?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This document, including the cover page, is three pages long. We only need to have the first paragraph translated, because that's what we used with this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have no problem with translation of the whole document because it's not a lengthy one. For better understanding we should have the full text translated. The document will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D1119 shall be assigned Exhibit D364, marked for identification pending translation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can we have Exhibit D55 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, what we see on our screens at the moment is a document drafted by Viktor Bezruchenko, a Prosecution expert witness, and it's entitled "The Fall of Zepa," and it speaks about military developments. My question is: Did you have an opportunity to analyse this report? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I made a reference to this document when drafting my report. I used it when I was preparing the section of my report about Zepa to the effect that it allowed me to shorten it because I had no objection to the description and narrative of the military events as described by this expert in his report, and I made this note in my report. Instead, I focused on other documents relating to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. In Viktor Bezruchenko's report, would there be anything to add or subtract from the way he presented the events in the area of Zepa based on documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I also drafted a report about Zepa, and I emphasized that I accepted everything that was mentioned in this report and that I will add only those things that I deem to be significant about Zepa. This is exactly what I did in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up D60. Thank you. I would like to thank the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Now we can see here a document. In handwriting you can see that it was drafted by the communication centre of the General Staff of the BiH army. It was dispatched on the 18th of July, 1995, from Kakanj at 1716 hours. I am going to quote some parts of the document. "General Delic, Protected." Under 1: "I have just been talking to General Smith. Perhaps I could have women, children, and the elderly from Zepa evacuated by UNPROFOR. Would you accept this? "Perhaps in this case we could insert a brigade (or a battalion) of soldiers to Zepa across the forest-path and thus continue the combat with more success. These men from Zepa say that they could find between 500 and 100 volunteers (Muderis is from Zepa)." Under 3: "Groups should also be inserted into Gorazde (over land). This would be a great encouragement. There are people interested." Under 4: "An evacuation plan for the population of Zepa has been made here in case items 1 and 2 above fail. I'm sending it to you. "I am waiting for your answers to the above. "Sarajevo, 18 July 1995. "Salem. "A. I." Mr. Skrbic, have you ever seen this document before? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Were you able to conclude who signed the document, i.e., whom sent the document to whom? Could you conclude that based on the body of the text and the contents of the document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no doubt about the fact that the text was sent by the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, to the chief of the General Staff of the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The text was sent on the 18th of July, 1995, as you can see on the document. Can you tell us whether the state and military leaderships in the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the army, respectively, consider an evacuation of the population from Zepa to the territory under the control of the BH army? Were plans drafted to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no doubt about that either. The plan was drafted after the fall of the 28th Division and the evacuation of the population from Srebrenica. The only thing that is strange about this document is the fact that the president of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, who was also the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, asked his main person in command of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina as to what he thinks and as to what he proposes. He is in a position to give him orders. He should not be seeking his approval or opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. What we see under number 1, is it Mr. Izetbegovic's report to General Delic about his conversations with UNPROFOR about that topic? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is certain because President Izetbegovic says here that he has just finished a conversation with UNPROFOR. As far as I can tell, that conversation involved the commander of UNPROFOR for Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is no doubt about the topic of the conversation. It is very clear that they discussed the possibility of evacuating the population from Zepa. As you can see from the document, the UNPROFOR commander suggested that he could be of assistance with the evacuation of women, children, and the elderly because the UNPROFOR forces could assist. It is quite unlikely that he would have suggested something else that was beyond the capabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the document say that the evacuation should be assisted by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. UNPROFOR would be organising and carrying out the evacuation that General Smith proposed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the document show that the president of the state was in favour of the evacuation of women, children, and the elderly, but at the same time he wanted to continue fighting in the enclaves, i.e., he wanted the forces of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina to continue fighting in the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This can be tied up with my testimony provided yesterday. Under 488 [as interpreted] of the main idea, it was suggested what could happen to them, that they would be breaking through with the general population on their back. Obviously, this is an attempt to lift off the burden from the army in Zepa to allow them to continue fighting. It is stated here that it would be good to have 500 to 1.000 volunteers joining them. That's according to President Izetbegovic. They should be sent to Zepa. It says here that there are already 500 to 1.000 people from Zepa. I suppose that he received this information from a certain Muderis who is mentioned here in the document and who is a native of Zepa. He suggests that in order to achieve a good effect it would be good to insert some of the forces into Gorazde over land, of course. He also thinks that if the evacuation should indeed take place, that it should be carried out through the forest-path. This points to the fact that the forest-paths in question had already been used before for the supply of the units in Zepa. Those forest-paths were not unknown even to the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you said, after reading this document, that it speaks about 500 to 1.000 volunteers. Could we please enlarge the second paragraph of the document. The -- yes, especially that part. That's very helpful. Could you tell us what is written there: 500 to 1.000; or 100, as it states in the translation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this -- the way I read it is 500-1- -- or this could be translated as 500 to something, but there is something wrong here. This must be a typo. It -- it is impossible to provide a range without the lowest figure to the highest figure. A range does not exist if it is not marked by the two extreme figures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps the interpreters interpreted the 1 behind the dash, the first dash, as an I; it could mean "and." But after that we have three 0s. Is it possible to interpret this number as 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't think that this figure should be -- or could be interpreted as "100," because the first figure that we see is 500, and when you're talking about a range from 500 to something else, to another figure, that next figure, the second figure, must be higher than the first figure, which in this case is 500.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would agree with that, especially because we see three 0s. Thank you for clarification. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And now I would like to call up D55, page 16. Thank you. Paragraph 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is again the report of Mr. Bezruchenko.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President. This is Mr. Bezruchenko's report, entitled "The Fall of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading paragraph 60. I'm quoting: "The meeting between VRS General Tolimir and Zepa civilian leaders Hamdija Torlak and Mujo Omanovic took place on the 13 July at 1200 hours. According to Tolimir's account, the agenda of the meeting included 'demilitarisation of the enclave and freedom of movement of the civilian population in accordance with Geneva Conventions as of 12 August 1949.' According to the document, representatives of the local government in Zepa stated that they were authorised 'to resolve the problem of Zepa' with the following guarantees: Three days for consultations with the population and the leadership in Sarajevo; movement out of all civilians and militarily able-bodied men; evacuation to be completed with the presence of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and military observers; guarantees of security during the movement across the RS territory; a possibility to stay in Zepa for all those who wish to stay there. Tolimir rejected the request for three days for consultations and demanded that the evacuation begins at 1500 hours. The only alternative was military force. Tolimir also demanded that all militarily able-bodied men should be registered and exchanged for 'our war prisoners in Muslim prisons.' Tolimir's assessment was that ..." and so on and so forth. My question to you, Mr. Skrbic, is this: You have read the report on "The Fall of Zepa" and adopted it fully. Can you tell us when the negotiations started for the civilian population to leave Zepa under the conditions stated in this document? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the documents that I had at my disposal, the first round of negotiations dealt with the problems of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We saw that Alija's letter to Delic was dated the 18th. What about the Muslim delegation's behaviour; was there duplicity in their behaviour? On the one hand, they negotiated the evacuation, and on the other hand they wanted to continue fighting. What is your comment to that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was duplicity in their conduct. However, I, as a military expert, do not understand how come that the Supreme Commander of the armed forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, after the crash of the 28th Division and after the 285th Brigade was cut off from its mother unit which is even further from the units of the 2nd Corps than the 28th Division, how can he think that it is still possible to continue fighting within the context that was creating when the 28th Division collapsed?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, please have a look at the fourth line in paragraph 60, which starts after the date 12th of August, 1949. And I quote: "According to the document, representatives of the local government in Zepa stated that they were authorised 'to resolve the problem of Zepa' with the following guarantees ..." My question is as follows: Did representatives -- or were Zepa representatives authorised to deal with the problem when they went to negotiate with the side that they were at war with?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That part of the report concerns political issues more than military ones, and in the report, at the beginning of the report, I emphasized the fact that I would try to avoid, to the extent that was possible, political issues, dealing with political issues, because given my understanding of politics, everything is possible in politics. But when you have an armed conflict, not everything is possible according to military doctrine. But if they say that they were authorised, and given my understanding of politics and political issues, local politicians have the authority to take care of their people. And this is, in fact, the reason for which the people elect such representatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as I will now be moving on to another question, I suggest that it might be an appropriate time for a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed, you are right, Mr. Tolimir. We must have our first break now, and we will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please see D51. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we can see here that on the basis of the negotiations that we were discussing, an agreement was signed on the disarmament of the able-bodied population in the Zepa enclave. Have you seen this agreement and have you seen that it refers to the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document. But as far as I can remember, I didn't refer to this document in my report. But I can't claim that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll see later that this document on the fall of Zepa states the following -- well, I'll quote from the first paragraph: "On the 24th of July, 1995, the following agreement was reached between Rajko Kusic on one side and Hamdija Torlak on the other, in the presence of UNPROFOR representative Semjon Dudnik." And then we have a number of items. Item 1: "A cease-fire between the parties to the conflict shall be complemented immediately." Item 2: "Avdo Palic shall issue an order to his troops to withdraw from the defence line and refugee groups together with the population and from the centre of settlement/villages, and not to try to across illegally through the territory of Republika Srpska." Next paragraph: "The civilian and able-bodied population of Zepa shall assemble around the UNPROFOR base in Zepa, which will be assigned to the Army of Republika Srpska, that the units under the command of Avdo Palic have accepted the truce and will not try to take advantage of it." Thank you. Five: "Avdo Palic shall start disarming his units immediately, and all the weapons shall be handed over to the VRS representative in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa." Six: "Avdo Palic shall indicate all the mined areas and they shall be cleared in the presence of a joint commission and UNPROFOR." Seven: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August, 1949, and the Additional Protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Eight: "The able-bodied population of Zepa shall be registered and accommodated in a holding centre which is to be under the control of the ICRC until the release of all captive VRS members and other Serbs who are in prisons in territory controlled by the army under the command of Rasim Delic." Nine: "The ICRC shall transport the able-bodied population of Zepa from the holding centres to territory under the control of Rasim Delic's army," I can't read this word.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At the same time."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "... at the same time as all captive VRS members and other Serbs who are in prison in territory controlled by the army under the command of Rasim Delic are released and transported to Republika Srpska." Ten: "The UNPROFOR, the ICRC, the UNHCR, and other international humanitarian organisations in co-operation with the Army of Republika Srpska shall enable the transport of the civilian population from Zepa to territory under the control of Rasim Delic's army or to third countries of their choice in accordance with the Geneva Conventions of the 12th of August, 1949." The agreement of the 12th of August, 1949, the agreement shall enter into force immediately after having been signed. Could we scroll up a bit so that we can see the signatures. We can see Rajko Kusic's signature from the Light Infantry Brigade; Dudnik, Semjon, UNPROFOR representative; Hamdija Torlak, a representative of the civilian authorities; Ratko Mladic also signed the document as the VRS commander. And this was on the 24th of July, 1995. My question is as follows: Since this agreement was entered -- was signed, did you see in the documents that the population did leave Zepa and went to territory under the control of the ABiH, which is in accordance with the items referred to in the agreement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could see, the evacuation of the population from Zepa had not yet been organised, but there were evacuations of certain individuals and certain groups a lot earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And when did you see that all the population from Zepa was being evacuated to territory under the control of the ABiH? Did you see that in the documents on the fall of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I stopped the witness because he was starting too early. We were still listening to the interpreters. Now you have the floor to give your answer. Please pause after the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'm really making an effort but sometimes I slip up. On the basis of the documents available, it could be seen that the final evacuation was completed - the evacuation from Zepa - on the 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's see when the evacuation started.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D55, item 105. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see item 105 of the report. It says: "UNPROFOR started evacuation from Zepa on the 25th of July. In the afternoon of the 25th of July, French Battalion 2 of Sector Sarajevo sent a medevac convoy to Zepa for the evacuation of the wounded. The convoy returned to Sarajevo next morning and brought 151 people. 29 seriously injured immediately received medical treatment in Sarajevo hospital. Around midnight, the VRS, using their own buses, evacuated around 1.000 people ..." Mr. Skrbic, did this evacuation start one day after the signing of the agreement? That is to say, did it start on the 25th? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that is quite logical because the agreement was signed on the previous day and the provisions of the agreement can enter into forces immediately after the agreement has been signed. But the implementation of the agreement and the entry into force aren't the same things. The implementation could not take place immediately, so it took place on the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we have this document in front of us, could we please take a look at 108, paragraph 108 on "The Fall of Zepa." It's on the next page. Since the evacuation of the population of Zepa started pursuant to the agreement and as stated in Bezruchenko's report, did you see anything about this in the document that you reviewed? You told us the date when it ended.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, I stop you again. Please wait. Please wait. Don't start immediately after you have heard Mr. Tolimir. You are using the same language but we can't follow. Please wait. Now your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you once again. Yes, according to the document that I had at my disposal, the evacuation was finalised on the 27th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you tell us, In accordance with the agreement was the disarming of the BH army in Zepa conducted, and did they surrender their weapons to UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could deduce from the documents, there was no disarming and there was no surrender of weapons by members of the 285th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, if only a part of an agreement is implemented and we have the entire population of Zepa departing from the area and you only have soldiers staying in the territory refusing to surrender their weapons, how is this situation treated in war time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That can be an indication of only one thing and that is that members of the 285th Brigade did not want to surrender and did not want to disarm because their intention was to continue with the armed resistance but only under altered circumstances, and they were obviously prepared to continue their resistance according to the principles of guerrilla warfare, because there was no other way for them to carry out combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Was that a demand imposed on them by their superior command? Have you seen anything in the documents to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the previous session we saw that the Supreme Commander demanded that the chief of Main Staff maintain, as one of the priorities, armed combat and armed resistance, and everything else stems from that priority number one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Let us now see what the brigade commander thought about these activities of his brigade and of the attitude of the presidency towards their brigade. Let's look at item 108, which reads: "Following the meeting between General Smith and Hamdija Torlak on the 26th July, 285th Brigade Commander Avdo Palic sent a dramatic appeal for help to BH President Alija Izetbegovic and General Staff Commander Rasim Delic." I quote the appeal sent by Mr. Avdo Palic. [As read] "Mr. President, at about 2100 hours, negotiations in Boksanica (Rogatica) at which General Smith; Torlak, Hamdija; President of the Executive Board of Zepa; and the war criminal Ratko Mladic were present has ended. As General Suvalic informed me today, during these negotiations an agreement about the exchange of 'all for all' was to be accepted also by our side. Minister Muratovic was supposed to be present at these negotiations but he was not, because security was not guaranteed for him. General Suvalic also informed me about this. During negotiations, General Smith told us that our side did not accept the agreement about the exchange of 'all for all' and that our side was seeking some additional concessions. Hamdija Torlak remained at the place of negotiations in Boksanica, and he was told that if we were prepared for the exchange of 'all for all' during the night or until 0800 hours in the morning General Smith will let us know so that a plan of helicopter evacuation could be prepared. "President, on behalf of my brigade which is on the verge of nervous breakdown, please arrange for our side to accept the agreement and free us from torture. We cannot believe that this problem looks like you will not solve it. If this problem is not resolved in the course of tomorrow, I must make a decision tomorrow to make a breakthrough towards you with 2.000 men and 10.000 rounds of ammunition, and we'll see who will manage to cross. And you have the picture of Srebrenica and the intelligence that we are blocked from all sides and that we have no salvation, despite that we move to break through. Tomorrow the evacuation of the civilians will be over and UNPROFOR will pull out immediately so that as of tomorrow we will be probably left to our own devices. "President, I ask you in the name of soldiers who have been fighting for the last 15 days like lions. I ask in the name of the fallen soldiers, and in my ranks I have sons or parents of those who have died. I ask you in the name of the evacuated families and children who are eagerly awaiting to reunite with their fathers who have remained on the Zepa mountain to be slaughtered or annihilated in any other way. I ask you again in the name of my soldiers to make it possible for us to defend Bosnia in some other battle-fields, to liberate it, and to die like people. Do not let us die of hunger, of most common diseases, because we do not have a single doctor but already have sick people ..." so on and so forth. Now my question is: Was the brigade's plan to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Tolimir, please repeat the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters didn't catch your question. Please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, the brigade commander, the Zepa Brigade commander, Mr. Palic, did he want this agreement to be implemented, and did he want all the soldiers and the entire Zepa civilian population be evacuated to the territory under the BH control? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no doubt about it. One can clearly see here that the commander of the 285th Brigade stated that he, as a local commander, was prepared to evacuate himself and his troops alongside the civilian population, to surrender their weapons, and to be exchanged according to the principle "all for all." However, it is also clear that his superior command based in Sarajevo, which is the highest level of command, including the Commander-In-Chief, did not approve the exchange of prisoners of war on the principle of "all for all." Had they approved it, that would greatly facilitate the situation for Palic and he would have been able to know what kind of decision he needed to take. This was a dramatic situation in which Commander Palic found himself, because he was put in a position to make independent decisions and to communicate directly with the Supreme Command because he no longer had his own superior command, which was the command of the 28th Division, with whom he lost all communications as of the night between the 11th and the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have document 1D1103 in e-court. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see that this is a book entitled "The Srebrenica Massacre: Evidence, Context, Politics." My question is: Did you have an opportunity to read this book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. But at the time when I was already halfway through my report. I'd like to add that I attended a promotion of this book at the book fair in Belgrade on the 26th or 27th October of last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 7 in English and page 11 in Serbian, and this is an introductory or forward written by Phillip Corwin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you tell us who Phillip Corwin is, and what position did he hold in July of 1995? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please switch off your microphone during your private conversation. Your answer now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to admit that I don't know who Phillip Corwin is but I know what he did in the relevant period that includes the events in Zepa. Phillip Corwin was the head of the G5 organ at the UNPROFOR command for Bosnia-Herzegovina in Sarajevo. According to the standards applicable by western armies and NATO, G5 is an organ for civilian affairs and deals with civilian matters and co-ordinates military and civilian matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at line 5 -- or, rather, line 6, the sentence which starts after "1992 to 1995," it says: [As read] "I expressed the wish that there could have been, and must be, more balance -- some balance in telling the story of what actually happened in Srebrenica and in all of former Yugoslavia if we are to learn from our experience." My question is this: Since you have reviewed the documents produced by UNPROFOR and various commissions that were active in the area, did you notice that anyone maintained this kind of views and did you hear anything about lessons to be learned? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I would like to note that I, personally, I do not favour any balances on the road to finding the truth. If you are seeking truth and if you accept the principle of balance, then you have to make compromises. And there can be no compromises with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have page 12 in Serbian and page 8 in English, paragraph 2 in Serbian and paragraph 3 in English. Thank you. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And I'm going to quote the second paragraph in the Serbian version, which reads: [As read] "But the situation is more complicated than the public relations specialist would have us believe. That there were killings of noncombatants in Srebrenica as in all war zones is a certainty. And those who perpetrated them deserve to be condemned and prosecuted. And whether it was three or thirty or three hundred innocent civilians who were killed, it was a heinous crime. There can be no equivocation about that. At the same time, the facts presented in this volume make a very cogent argument that the figure of 8.000 killed, which is often bandied about in the international community, is an insupportable exaggeration. The true figure may be closer to 800." My question is this: I would like to comment -- I would like your comment on Phillip Corwin's position with regard to everything that he has stated.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can comment on his position because this position confirms, first and foremost, the results of my own analysis. Moreover, it also confirms the fact that there were civilian casualties. And I am not disputing that. As a military expert and as a commander, I know that whenever there is fighting in urban areas or in settled areas it is impossible to avoid collateral casualties among the civilian population. When it comes to the responsibility for civilian casualties when there is fighting in urban areas, that responsibility primarily lies on the troops that are defending such areas. Why is that so? If they are looking after their people, they are duty-bound to carry out their activities from the sectors and areas where there is no civilian population present. And this is the best way how to protect the civilian population. My personal experience arises from the time when I became brigade commander. That is when I found supporting artillery units in settled areas. I immediately issued an order for those units to be moved out from those settled areas, because every time they provided artillery support to my brigade, a counterattack would ensue on the part of the 5th Corps units, which is only understandable. What they wanted to do was to neutralise the activity of my own artillery. As a result, instead of targeting and hitting my own artillery, at least 30 per cent of their shells hit civilian facilities close to my own artillery positions. That is why I decided to move my artillery units out of the settled area. That was the way I showed concern for possible civilian casualties. I would kindly ask the Trial Chamber to allow me to say something else about civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It must be the decision of Mr. Tolimir. He is interviewing you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, yes, you can say whatever you want. Try and be concise, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to confirm everything that I have stated so far. In situations when you -- there is fighting going on in urbanised areas, it is impossible to avoid civilian casualties. I would like to quote the last operation in Iraq, when the defence minister of the United States of America Donald Rumsfeld talked to the commander of the airforce which carried out air-strikes on urban areas, and he asked to be informed about every air-strike, which, according to their estimate, would result in over 30 per cent of civilian casualties. He wanted to be informed in advance so as to be able to make an appropriate decision. He was informed about such air-strikes 50 times. All those air-strikes were approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, you are an expert to testify about the war in the former Yugoslavia, not about a war or any military activities in another area, like Iraq. Please comment on -- please use your knowledge about the war in the former Yugoslavia. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up page 14 in Serbian and page 12 in English. I am looking for paragraph 2 in the English version. Thank you. We can now see the document. I am going to -- It's page 11 in English. I apologise. Thank you, Aleksandar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I am going to read now. I am reading from the third paragraph in the Serbian version, and I quote: "Back to military concerns. It was evident by July 1995 that the Bosnian Serb army could not continue to allow five enemy bases to exist behind its front lines. Mind you, I'm not speaking about the humanitarian issues here, because I've never, and will never, condone the slaughter of civilians. However, it would be irresponsible to ignore the military aspect of the campaign in Eastern Bosnia when discussing Srebrenica, just as it would be foolish to ignore the historical process that led up to the events of July 1995." Mr. Skrbic, in your expert report on Srebrenica, did you also present the same or similar position? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I was primarily concerned with military issues in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. How does this position presented by Mr. Corwin fit within your own position and the findings of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Corwin's position only confirms what I presented in my own expert report, and it supports my positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up page 12 in Serbian, the last paragraph. Page 9, paragraph 2, in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can now see the last paragraph. I'm reading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before you read it, I have to clarify one legal matter. I was just -- my attention was drawn to one part of this document, where it says: "No part of this publication may be reproduced without prior written permission of the publisher." When we receive such a document into evidence, it will be in the public domain. Can you clarify if you have asked for such a permission? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as far as I am familiar with copyright laws, this is a book, and if anything is quoted from a book, one should mention the author, the title of the book. In other words, one should follow the customary procedure. All of these documents can be found in an electronic form, so there is no need to seek a special approval, because this reproduction is not a commercial reproduction. It is only used as evidence in this case. And since in this case we do not tender into evidence any hard copies, which is a normal copy for a book, the electronic form is acceptable, and both copies were downloaded from the internet. What you have just read out, Mr. President, is something that each publication contains, which means that for every single book we should seek approval from the author to allow us to present his work in this courtroom. What I'm saying here is that this is a usual clause that is included in every publication of this nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir and Mr. Gajic, it was just a warning so that you are aware of the situation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's read. I'm going to quote Mr. Corwin's words word for word: [As read] "What happened in Srebrenica was not a single large massacre of Muslims by Serbs, but, rather, a series of very bloody attacks and counterattacks over a three-year period which reached a crescendo in 1995. And the number of Muslims executed in the last battle of Srebrenica, as former BBC report Jonathan Rooper has pointed out, was most likely in the hundreds, not in the thousands. Moreover, it is likely that the number of Muslim dead was probably no more than number of Serbs that had been killed in Srebrenica and its environs during the preceding years by Bosnian Commander Naser Oric and his predatory gangs." My question to you is this: When it comes to this position proffered by Mr. Corwin, does it fit within your own analysis?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This position fully coincides with the results of my own analysis, because the results of my analysis have shown, quite unambiguously, that Muslim losses during Krivaja 95 Operation and after it certainly cannot be expressed in the thousands. Mr. Jonathan Rooper says that the losses were in the hundreds, and I'm familiar with that because that information was published in a reputable western magazine "Defense & Foreign Affairs," in an article entitled "The Icon of Srebrenica."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could the e-court produce page 88 in the document in Serbian, 101 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We will see Mr. Jonathan Rooper's article entitled "The Numbers Game."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
