utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 89 in Serbian, 103 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The last paragraph on page 103 in the English version. It says: [As read] "The current chapter looks closely at the numbers, data, and explores them against the back-drop of the official version of what happened in the weeks after the fall of the Srebrenica safe area. It will show that rather than Srebrenica being the worst atrocity in Europe since the Second World War, 'a stain on our collective conscious,' in which 8.000 men and boys were murdered, it is the official version that is at odds with key facts and fails to provide a consistent and coherent representation of the relevant events in 1995." My question: Does this position provided by the author fit in with your conclusions about the movement of the population of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does fit in, and there are no two ways about it. There's no doubt about this position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we look at page 90 in the same document, paragraph 3 in Serbian. And page 103, the last paragraph in the English version of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the second paragraph. I am reading from the chapter entitled "Origins of the Massacre Allegations." [As read] "The original ballpark estimates for the number of persons who might have died following the fall of Srebrenica corresponded closely to the list of some 8.000 'missing' persons. The United Nations and other independent observers witnessed fierce fighting in which both sides lost a considerable number of people. It is also known that they were killed in the territory around Tuzla and Zepa. It is impossible to determine exactly how many people fall under which category, but since we know that there are a lot of people in each of the categories, this goes to show that the number of missing was much lower than alleged. There are strong reasons for skepticism with regard to the allegations about massacre. Over the years, new information have appeared. The official version of the events, which was established in 1995, has in the meantime been slightly modified, but now it seems less credible. The most important thing about the figures is the fact that there is something wrong with the maths." Thank you. And my question is this: Since on a number of occasions you used the term "mathematics," could you please tell us whether this also supports your analysis of numbers and mathematics? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This confirms that my research and my calculations, my calculations of the number of Muslims who left Srebrenica in various manners and the number of those who were in Srebrenica before the Krivaja 95 operation, my research and my calculations were correct, and the method I followed was the right one. As it is here stated, that it is expected that the official version will be changed, I also expect that following my analysis this change will occur sooner than expected by this gentleman, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since Mr. Jonathan Rooper speaks about "The Numbers Game," could you please tell me what he means when he says "game"? Is he speaking about real numbers or is he speaking about manipulating numbers? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the very word -- the very expression "the numbers game" implies that information is being manipulated, numbers are being manipulated, and such information is then being disseminated to the public. This is also shown by the fact that Mr. Jonathan Rooper is here comparing a list of the missing, or, rather, he's comparing the concept of those who are missing and those who were killed, and no such comparison is possible because "missing people" has a very precise meaning, and "people who were killed" also refers to a very precisely and defined category of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page 90, paragraph 3. It's the last paragraph in the English version. Thank you. I apologise, my mistake. Page 92, paragraph three. It's page 106 in the English version. It's the last paragraph. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [As read] "If we take into account all these factors - in the course of moving out from the protected zone of Srebrenica 8.000 men and boys were massacred - and taking into account these factors, the population of the protected zone before its fall should have been significantly greater than 66.000, which is a figure far higher than any estimate hitherto provided; in fact, there is in fact relatively little variation given in the accounts which presume that massacres took place. They agree that the majority of Srebrenica's population went to Potocari (estimates range from 24.000 to 27.000) and a minority went to the column that set of for Tuzla (estimates range from 10- to 15.000). The consensus total for Srebrenica safe -- for the Srebrenica safe area inhabitants was approximately 37.000 persons in all, made up of some 25.000 who went to Potocari and 12.000 who left in the column." My question, Mr. Skrbic, is as follows: How do these figures fit in with your analysis? How do you view them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The allegations in this paragraph fully support my analysis, fully agree with it. It is true that perhaps there were 37.000 inhabitants in Srebrenica at the time of the initial attack on Srebrenica, and this is possible to demonstrate quite simply. It's possible to calculate this quite simply. If you have the figure of 25.000 refugees who went to Potocari and then you add to that figure the higher number of 10- to 15.000 who attempted a breakthrough, then you have 40.000, which means that at the time of the attack on Srebrenica there were 40.000. But if we have real doubts about the upper figure of 15.000, since the lower figure is 10.000, well in that case it's more probable that there were fewer than 40.000 inhabitants in Srebrenica at the time of the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could 1D1103 please be admitted into evidence, and pages 1, pages 11 to 15, 88 to 132 in the Serbian version. And pages 1 and 7 to 12 in the English version, as well as 101 to 152, also in the English version. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know that we're dealing with a number of different authors that contributed to this particular publication, if I've got it right, and what I'd like, if General Tolimir is able to do, is to clarify for the record which pages correspond with which authors, just so that it's clear for the record. And secondly, it will also be clearer for the record when the relative pieces were written or -- and clearly by whom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And I -- in addition, I would like to know, if you really tender many more pages than we have seen on the screen and you dealt with, especially the pages 101 up to 152. We didn't see 51 pages. But, Mr. Gajic, please help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. First I would like to answer your question. Of course, we did not show all the entire article. If we had gone through the entire article, that would really have taken up a lot of time. We used the numbers referred to by Mr. Tolimir, and these numbers relate to Phillip Corwin's introduction and to Mr. Rooper's article entitled "The Numbers Game." If the entire article is admitted, we can then assess the context that gave rise to the article. We can see the context within which the paragraphs appear, and the footnotes themselves, at the end of the article. So these footnotes appear at the end of the book. That is how it was laid out. So, in our opinion, admitting these two articles would be of assistance to the Trial Chamber and to the parties. It would help us to assess these two articles and the extracts that we used through the witness. To go through the entire article would have taken up a lot of time, and in our opinion this was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To fully understand your submission, Mr. Gajic, pages 1 as well as pages 11 to 15 in the B/C/S version, and pages 1 and, in addition, 7 to 12 in the English version: These are the pages from the forward; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour. Page 1 in the title page of the book. Pages 7 to 12 are Phillip Corwin's introduction. Pages 88 to 132 are the pages where we can find the article "The Numbers Game" in the Serbian version. And pages 101 to 152 represent the English version of that article. And let me just add that for the sake of our presentation we uploaded the entire book so that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution could see how these articles were published. But, naturally, if the Chamber accepts our request to admit these articles into evidence, we'll have 65 ter numbers or a different 65 ter number for these documents. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic, Mr. Vanderpuye asked you when the article of Mr. Jonathan Rooper was written or edited or published.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we see page 3 in the English version. No, I apologise. The translation was published in 2011. I know that. And this book was published a few years earlier in English. I'll check the year now. That's why I sat down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For a better understanding of the content, it would be helpful to know when it was written. Mr. Vanderpuye, are you satisfied with these additional information?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am very satisfied, Mr. President. The only issue, obviously, is the date of publication with respect to this; but otherwise there's no problem, and I think the record is clear as to what the Defence is relying on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, on page 2 in the English version it says "Licensed in 2011." This is an internet publication. I believe that this book was accessible to the public at an even earlier date. I'll do my best to check when this book was published as a hard copy and I will try to provide you with that information tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Gajic and Mr. Tolimir, I would appreciate if you would upload these two articles, that means the forward and the article, as a different document into e-court so that that one will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Your Honour. That will be done as soon as possible in the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Very well. It will be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the referenced articles of the 65 ter document 1D1103 shall be assigned Exhibit D365. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could 1D1103 please be -- 1D115, the public version of the report from Ratko Skrbic, could that document please be admitted into evidence. The title is "Srebrenica and Zepa." Thank you. I would also ask that 1D1063 also be admitted into evidence, and this is the confidential version of the same report. And the public version on the report of the movement of the population, 1D114, could that also be admitted into evidence as well --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat the last number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think most of the numbers are not correctly recorded. I would kindly ask Mr. Gajic to give us the correct numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The report from Mr. Ratko Skrbic entitled "Srebrenica and Zepa," the public version, is 1D1115. The confidential version has the following number: 1D1063. Mr. Ratko Skrbic's report, "The Movement of the Population of Srebrenica," the number of the public version for that report is 1D1114. And the confidential 65 ter version is 1D1063.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This can't be correct because that number relates to the first report. You have given us twice the same number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. It should be 1D1064, the last one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that the Prosecution filed a notice on the 20th of January, 2012, and the Prosecution is telling us that the Prosecution doesn't accept the expert report of Colonel Ratko Skrbic. What is your position, Mr. Vanderpuye, to the request to admit these documents into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to the request to admit the documents into evidence, Mr. President, at this time we don't have an objection. Obviously throughout the course of the examination of Mr. Skrbic our position may change depending upon how he responds or what his evidence is with respect to his methodology and so on. But for the moment we don't have an objection to the Trial Chamber receiving them, at least preliminarily, because I think at this point, at this particular juncture, they establish, at least on their face, enough of a basis for their preliminary admission. That's a separate question, I think, and I will probably ask the Court to revisit that at the end of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Gajic, 1D1064, under seal, was not released, and it's not available in e-court yet. Please check that. I would suggest that we mark all four documents for identification and we postpone the final decision on the admission of the two reports in confidential and public redacted version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 1D1115 shall be assigned Exhibit D366. 65 ter document 1D1063 shall be assigned Exhibit D367 under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter document 1D1114 shall be assigned Exhibit D368.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And 65 ter document 1D1064 shall be assigned Exhibit D369 under seal, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it seems that sometimes fatigue takes its toll. I made a mistake when I told you the last number, and did it twice. Mr. Ratko Skrbic's confidential report on "The Movement of the Population of Srebrenica and Zepa" is, in fact, 1D1062. It is entirely my mistake. I said that the number was erroneously 1D1064.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: 1D1062 will be D369, marked for identification, under seal. Now we have it on the record. Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic, our expert, for coming here and for explaining his views and presenting his expert work. I wish him success in his work, I wish him good health, and may God be with him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Defence team, Mr. President, I would like to express my gratitude to all participants in the proceedings, and I would just like to end by saying that the Defence has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Vanderpuye, I think it would be convenient for you - and for all others - to have the second break now, and after the break you shall commence your cross-examination. We must have our second break now and will resume five minutes before 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Our apologies for the delayed return to the courtroom. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just two short questions. The CDs of the video-clip admitted as D280 have been provided to the Registry and we would kindly ask for it to be finally admitted fully into evidence. And the second thing: D349, marked for identification, and following the guidance given by the Trial Chamber on the 31st of January, we requested a revision of the translation. We received it yesterday and it has been uploaded into e-court; and as a result, we would like that to be finally admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Both documents are now received into evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye, your cross-examination, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good afternoon to you, Mr. Skrbic. On behalf of the Prosecution, I will be asking you some questions in relation to your direct examination. And if there's anything that I ask you that's not clear, please let me know and I will try and phrase it in a way that we can better understand one another. Because the interpreters have to keep up with us, I'll ask you to try and speak a little bit slower than you might ordinarily, and I'll try to do the same, although I'm not always good at it. What I would like to know right off the bat is: You presented your report to General Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Through his legal advisor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And he agrees with the conclusions that you draw in your report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that since he accepted me as a witness here, I believe that he agrees with my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. But surely you have spoken with the Defence before coming here to testify in this case.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you've spoken to them with respect to the preparation of your report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I've spoken with them about the preparation of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Of course. And when did that happen? When did you speak with the Defence for the first time regarding your report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the first telephone call came from Mr. Gajic sometime in May or June this year. He wanted me to come over, that we become acquainted, and to explain to me what would potentially be required of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did you meet with Mr. Gajic to discuss what would be required of you after that first phone call?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we met, because in this telephone conversation I didn't quite understand what this was all about and I wanted to learn more details about what my terms of reference would be. After that, Mr. Gajic and I met and in this personal conversation it was imparted precisely upon me what my role would be, not what I am supposed to do. After that, I asked to be given some time to think it over and to decide whether I am able to do that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: It was just a clarification. If you go to page 60, line 19, you have just said: "The first telephone call came from Mr. Gajic sometime in May or June this year." Can you clarify which May and June you are referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course not this year. It was last year. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You said that you met with him to discuss the terms of reference. Did you meet with him subsequently, after that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us about how many times you met with Mr. Gajic or any member of the Defence before you testified -- or began your testimony here, rather?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't meet anyone else from General Tolimir's Defence team apart from Mr. Gajic. Secondly, I cannot tell you exactly, but after that initial conversation we met perhaps four or six times more.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And at those meetings, you also discussed the terms of reference for your engagement or did you discuss other matters particular to the report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't discuss what was to be contained in my report. At those meetings, Mr. Gajic would provide me with the necessary documents that I had requested to be supplied to me, and it was me who presented to Mr. Gajic what my wishes were, what I think my report should look like. And I kindly asked him that if they are not satisfied with my views about the contents of the report, then I shouldn't be preparing the report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Great. Thank you very much for that clarification. You said that you received a number of documents from Mr. Gajic over the period of time that you were engaged prior to your testimony. And these are documents that you requested on your own, or these are documents that were offered you to look at?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, it was impossible for me to ask for specific documents. I asked to be supplied and provided with all the documents that he can offer that might be useful and which would fit with the idea of the report, as I explained to Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In terms of your explanation of the idea of the report, what did you say exactly? How did you convey this idea to Mr. Gajic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained to Mr. Gajic that based on the documents, my desire was to confirm or demonstrate whether it was accurate, the information that more than 7.000 able-bodied men were killed. That's as far as the first report is concerned. As for the second expert report, I asked him to be aware of my desire that on the basis of combat documents - primarily those coming from the BH army - I would like to put the events in Srebrenica and Zepa in the context of the conflict. In other words, the context of the conflict throughout the whole period. I wanted to avoid my report to be one-sided, and I didn't want to present the situation as being the situation in which only one side was active and the other side wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So I just want to be clear about something: With respect to the documents that you looked at in order to prepare your report on the population of Srebrenica, and your report - the military aspect of your report, the separate, second -- rather, the second report that you prepared - did you ask at all to see any specific documents?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never asked for any specific document. Because I can tell you that some documents I had received from General Miletic's Defence team, having worked as an investigator for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And these are documents that you incorporated in your report as well?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Some of them are.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you yourself were a member of the VRS during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you served in the 17 Kljuc Brigade during the conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. From 9th February, 1993, until 15th October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you also served in the 15th Bihac Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I was the commander of the 15th Bihac Brigade, and I was appointed to that position on the 15th November, 1993, and I remained in that post until the end of the conflict, i.e., until the Dayton Accords were signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned both on your direct and on cross-examination your association with the Defence of Radivoje Miletic. Is he somebody that you knew during the period of the war, between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew General Miletic. And I met him in 1990 because in that year we both started the course at the school of All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And did you know him -- did you keep in contact with him, I should say, throughout the war time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in touch with him during the war. We met only once, when he, with either the commander of the Main Staff or someone from the Main Staff, visited the western part of Republika Srpska and the 2nd Krajina Corps, and we met on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you kept in touch with him since you were engaged as a member of his Defence? I assume in the Popovic case you're talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether this case is called Popovic. Maybe that's the adopted name. This is case number IT-05-88-PT. But if you are referring to that Popovic case, then the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. You have the case number right as well. And what about General Tolimir. At the very beginning of his examination-in-chief, he mentioned that you knew each other well. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. General Tolimir attended the same high school that I did, only he was two years my senior, and we he met each other during our schooling at the high school.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And were you in contact with General Tolimir during the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any direct contact with him. I met him on one occasion in the course of the war for sure, perhaps twice. The first time I met him, he was with the commander of the Main Staff of the VRS. The commander was visiting the 2nd Krajina Corps on that occasion, and while visiting them he also visited my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And have you been in contact with him since the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the signing of the Dayton Agreement and the reorganisation of the VRS, as I have already said, I was transferred to the Main Staff, which is where I met General Tolimir. But as I was in the Main Staff only very briefly, we did not frequently have contact with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: How about after that, after you left the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I left in 1997 and went to the Army of Yugoslavia, I don't remember having met Tolimir again after I left. Not until I came to this courtroom, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Aside from not having met him, were you in contact with him during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was never in contact with him. I couldn't have been in contact with him if I did not meet him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because I wasn't a close friend of his. I didn't have his phone number, so it wasn't possible for me to use the phone to reach him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you do know each other well; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we know each other. But as for the expression "to know each other well," well, knowing someone well is very relative. Sometimes you might think that you know a person, but in fact you don't know that person sufficiently well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's true. I want to ask you a little bit about your population report, and I just want to see if I've got this right. Your report basically looked at certain figures for the population of Srebrenica before 1995; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's information in my report on the number of inhabitants even prior to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you compared those estimates against the number of registered people, refugees, from Srebrenica in August 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. And those estimates or, rather, calculations - they're not estimates because I didn't estimate the number of inhabitants, I used data from official documents, the information from local Muslim politicians and the civilian protection staff - and I can confirm that I compared those figures, too, with the numbers of refugees from Srebrenica after the month of July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I didn't mean to imply that your calculations were estimates. What I meant to say is that the data that you relied on were estimates. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. As I previously explained, they were documents from the Presidency of -- of the president of the Presidency of the Srebrenica municipality, and this data wasn't sent to the secretariat of Tuzla in the form of an assessment. This data was precise. I took this data to be precise and used that data to make my calculations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: One of the documents you relied on was a document showing the number of refugees that arrived in the area of Tuzla; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is it your testimony here today that that number that you relied on was an accurate number? Or was it an estimate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document that I used on the number of the population of Srebrenica that was categorised as refugees was a document taken from the debriefing of the Dutch government. And I am not making any claims. I took that document to be an accurate one. My opinion was not that it was an assessment, an estimate. I know that the report was compiled on the basis of a debriefing, and it was compiled as ordered by the Dutch parliament. And this, in fact, was organised by the Dutch institute for war documentation, if I remember this correctly. So I had no reason to doubt the accuracy or reliability of the information that was contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 7604 in e-court, please. Mr. President, I -- this is a document I have to add -- ask leave to add to the Prosecutor's 65 ter list. It is, essentially, the document that the Defence used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I heard a 65 ter number. I believe that this document is already in evidence. I think it was admitted during the testimony of Ms. Ewa Tabeau.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can you help us? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe that is correct, Mr. President, but there is -- there is another document that goes with this one that apparently isn't attached to it, but Mr. Gajic is correct. In substance this is right. There should be a number of pages that follow, which I don't think is part of the Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for the sake of the transcript, the first page is Defence Exhibit T314 [as interpreted]. It, in fact, consists of two pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said "D314"?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, the Prosecutor asks for leave to add the complete document to the 65 ter list. I take it, Mr. Tolimir, that you will not have any objection to that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. You are quite right. I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted, Mr. Vanderpuye, to add the entire document to the 65 ter exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I understand that the first page of this document was not uploaded. I have a copy of it. And I'd like to show that to the witness, if I could, on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please, with the assistance of the Usher. Please use the ELMO. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We don't have the signal from the ELMO, so unfortunately I don't have a second copy, and I can't read the document myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The ELMO is not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I can -- I can do it the old-fashioned way. I can just read the proposition that I want to make to the witness and see if he can respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But in that case you need the document back, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It should be given to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand I can do it a different way, yet. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What you have in front of you is a document from the Minister of Defence of the Netherlands. And it's addressed -- it's dated October 20th, 1995, and it is addressed to Mr. Goldstone, at that time a Prosecutor at this Tribunal. And in particular --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Vanderpuye, the witness is at the moment the only person in the courtroom who has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. I'm about to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It states -- it's addressed to Mr. Goldstone, and it says: "Herewith I send a document that was received during the debriefing of DutchBat about the registration of approximately 35.632 refugees from Srebrenica." It says: "If this number is correct, which is not sure, it can help to determine the number of missing and executed men from Srebrenica. Therefore, I think the document could be of interest to you." And it's signed accordingly. My question to you, Mr. Skrbic, is: One, have you seen this particular document before?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw this document was when I arrived in The Hague. Mr. Gajic showed it to me. I had never previously seen the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you've never seen this letter that I just read to you, have you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so your conclusion about the accuracy of the number of registered refugees from Srebrenica, is it impacted in any way by the fact that the Minister of Defence of the Netherlands himself is unsure of the accuracy of that number?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since this document, or, rather, the number 35.632 was officially included in the debriefing of the Dutch government, I have no need to have any doubts about it. I had no need to ask myself whether it was correct. This number was important for me, and I used it for the purposes of my analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, we've got that. My question is: Now that you see this letter, which says both that it's an approximation and, two, that it may not be -- it may not actually be right, does that impact your conclusion about the reliability of the number as you found it and used it in your report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't have an impact because I completed my analysis on the basis of data from various sources. There were numbers that had certain ranges. I had calculations from the lower figure and the high figure of given number ranges, so my report contains all the relevant examples. I believe there are eight or nine such examples in my report where all the relevant numbers that I could obtain were taken into account. And this number -- this conclusion that it's an approximate number could not have any effect on my final conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at the document as we have it in e-court. Can you see it on the screen in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's take a look at item A on this document. And you can see the number 35.632, and it says "approximately"; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you find any other number concerning the number of Srebrenica refugees following the fall of Srebrenica? Did you find any other document indicating the number of registered refugees? For the purposes of your report.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have any other documents on the number of refugees from Srebrenica because no one apart from the Sarajevo government, with the assistance of the WHO, registered the number of refugees from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So this is the number that you relied on to establish that 35.632 refugees from Srebrenica were registered, this is the only document; right?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. That is the basic document, the main document, and the main number that I relied on when drafting my analysis. And if I could also add the following: It's not just this document that refers to the number 35.632. I came across another document with the number 35.632. It's the article from Srebrenica, the Srebrenica Icon, in which Mr. Jonathan Rooper also mentions the number of 35.632, and that is why I had no reason to have any doubts about the reliability of that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Do you have any doubt now that you see that it's an estimate, an approximation, and it might not be accurate?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't have doubts about an official document. But apart from that, the conclusion that I reached isn't, in fact, that precise. In my conclusion I didn't say that 300 or 350 people were killed. All I did was draw a certain conclusion on the basis of information that was imprecise. I stated that the results of my analysis demonstrated that we could not speak about thousands of people being killed, so you can see for yourself that I didn't quite clearly state how many Muslims who were fit for military service were, in fact, killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I think I follow you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put one additional question in relation to this document. We see the number Mr. Vanderpuye was asking you about, 35.632, and then a breakdown with three other figures, one -- the first and the second line, these figures seem to be quite accurate. What is your opinion about the third figure, 6.500? Is that an accurate figure or an approximation, in your view, as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a precise figure and I think that is the case because the Special Rapporteur for Human Rights also mentioned that number when he reported on how many inhabitants left Srebrenica and where they had found accommodation. He, in fact, mentioned this number when referring to the people who had been provided with accommodation at the Tuzla airport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, I think it's time for adjournment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We have to continue tomorrow, in the morning, at 9.00 in this courtroom. And we adjourn for the day. And again, Mr. Skrbic, no contact, please, to either party during the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 9th day of February, 2012, at 9.00 a.m.
